Inside Ukraine

By: Anina Peens | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We are at Serit, the border between Romania and Ukraine amidst the increasing tension between Russia and Ukraine

Unique Selling Point:
We take a look at the conflict between Russia and Ukraine on the ground. We speak to locals, to understand the ongoing conflict amidst one of the greatest refugee crisises the world has seen since the end of world war 2.

Summary:
After Russia invaded Ukraine in February, Carte Blanche takes a closer look at the conflict between the two countries. Depicting the history to understand the tension and provide insider info and stories happening on the ground.

Script:


UKRAINE: THE WORLD’S WAR

VISUALS: Mariupol (Run first upsound under pics)

Upsound: I want to tell you about Mariupol… (PAUSE)

NEW VO: When we meet Julia in Siret, a Romanian town on the border with Ukraine, she asks us to hide her face. Like millions of others, she fled the Russian invasion and now fears for those she left behind in the besieged city of Mariupol.

Upsound (Just the beginning before fading for the translation) there is no cell phone reception in Mariupol, and people can’t scream for help.

NEW VO: There’s no cell phone reception, she says. People can’t scream for help. (PAUSE) Her husband was killed in a Russian rocket attack while trying to fetch water to bath their daughter.

Upsound: (Just the start before fading) People are not buried. Dead people are lying in the streets and their neighbours are burying them if possible.

NEW VO: Lots of people aren’t being buried, Julia says. Dead people are lying in the streets, their neighbours burying them where possible.

PAUSE FOR SCENE CHANGE

VISUALS: Anina travelling

NEW VO: We’ve been travelling in this region for over a week, now. Parts of the countryside here are so peaceful, its hard to believe places like Mariupol even exist. But you don’t have to be on the frontlines to see the impacts of Russia’s invasion. And the refugee crisis is only part of the problem.

Upsound: The refugees that is only 5 or 10% of problem of war (CUT)

NEW VO: And few know that better than Konstantine Kotchorian, a church pastor we meet in Ukraine’s Chernivtsi region.
Upsound: Most of the people who stay in that part where there is fighting now, that is a big problem because they stay in a poor situation. They don’t have eat and water. (please try work in reversal from later chat with Konstantine)

NEW VO: Konstanine and other church volunteers deliver aid to cities devastated in the conflict. (PAUSE) It’s a mammoth task: the latest reports say close to 400 thousand people are trapped without enough food and running water in Mariupol alone.

VISUALS: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rUnWv2945L8&t=26s

NEW VO: Many other towns are suffering a similar fate under Russia’s relentless shelling. This footage, released by Moscow shows naval missiles being fired at Ukrainian targets.

VISUALS: Combat (the more dramatic the better)

NEW VO: While ground forces from both sides battle for every inch of territory. Vladmir Putin’s invasion may have stalled, but the fighting remains fierce.

VISUALS AND Upsound: Explosions.

PAUSE FOR SCENE CHANGE

VISUALS: Anina travelling by train then window POV

NEW VO: It’s an unfolding tragedy that’s hard to reconcile with what we’re seeing in this part of the country. After a bitterly cold winter, it’s springtime – planting season. Nicolai Papuk is a wheat and soybean farmer.

Upsound: The land is hydrated.

NEW VO: The land is hydrated, he says.

Upsound: Where there is wheat now, there will be soybeans later.

NEW VO: Where there is wheat now, there will be soybeans later. (PAUSE)

VISUALS: Anina’s sunset walking shot

NEW VO: According to the World Food Programme, Ukraine and Russia produce 30% of the world’s wheat, 20% of its corn and an astonishing 75 to 80% of its sunflower oil.

LINK: Ukraine is called the breadbasket of Europe for a reason. The country’s rich soil and high rainfall create favourable farming conditions. (CUT)

NEW VO: But now, a combination of this ongoing war and international sanctions against Russia has governments bracing for a food crisis.

Upsound: We simply sow for the land to be sown. If it’s necessary to empty the field, then we do not know where to take and transfer the harvest.

NEW VO: We simply sow for the land to be sown, Nikolai says. If it’s necessary to empty the field, then we do not know where to take and transfer the harvest. (PAUSE)

VISUALS: Nikolai’s establisher.

NEW VO: In this time of war, farmers like Nicolai simply can’t sell what they’ve grown.

Upsound (with subs): All Ukrainian ports have been shut down, and they’ve been shut down since late February (CUT).

NEW VO: Russian-based, Andrey Sizov, is a grain analyst.

Upsound: Ukraine is also selling some.. shipping some green wheat and corn abroad, but it’s done not by sea terminals but by rail. And the rail capacity is very limited.

NEW VO: Ukraine is now exporting just one million tonnes of wheat and maize a month. In peacetime, that figure is closer to 7 million. (PAUSE) If the impact of that isn’t clear, consider this: a country like Egypt gets 85% of it grain from Ukraine, Lebanon around 80%. The World Food Programme recently announced its monthly expenses have increased by close to a billion rand because of rising fuel, food, and shipping costs – meaning it’s able to feed 4 million fewer people (may need a graphic)

PAUSE FOR SCENE CHANGE

VISUALS: More train and travel visuals, but now let’s see the military

NEW VO: Which is why, like Russia, Odessa is on our minds. Parts of Ukraine may be relatively calm, but everywhere are signs of the war raging to the East of us.

VISUALS: the anti-tank obstacles laid out on the roads (look like crosses)

NEW VO: Those metal crosses are laid out by city and village defenders in the hope they’ll cripple Russian tanks. They may be needed sooner rather than later in Odessa.

Link: Odessa has been bracing for a Russian onslaught since the start of the invasion. It’s a strategic port city on the Black Sea – a major grain exporting hub, with vital access to global trade routes.

NEW VO: In the past few days, it appeared peace talks had delivered a breakthrough: Moscow agreed to pull its forces back from Kyiv and reports suggest tensions have eased in the Ukrainian capital. But, here, it’s feared Russia’s strategy is merely changing and that Odessa may be the next Mariopul.

VISUALS: Mariupol desolation

NEW VO: And what would that mean for the lives of the thousands of people still here? And for the trickle of food still making its way out of this port? Our meeting with Julia provides a horrifying glimpse.

Upsound (refugee): There is emptiness in my soul now. I don’t have a home. (CUT) I should only think of my child now. I should live for her to give her a future.
NEW VO: There is emptiness in my soul now, she told us. I don’t have a home. I should only think of my child now. I should live for her to give her a future.
